text.title: Live Ticket Drafting (Shared-Screen Pattern) Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules with rationale + source for live-ticket-drafting-shared-screen-pattern. Includes terminal skip-this-methodology rule.

rule.statement: Ticket MUST be drafted in the shared screen during the elicitation session, not as a post-session write-up.
rule.rationale: Writing the ticket afterwards means reconstructing it from notes, and every gap in the notes gets filled with the BA's assumption rather than the contributor's answer, surfacing two weeks later as rework. Drafting live inverts the order: the act of writing is what exposes the missing acceptance criterion, and it exposes it while the only person who knows the answer is still in the room.

rule.statement: Each ticket MUST receive a verbal or chat sign-off from the contributor before the session ends; deferred sign-off is forbidden.
rule.rationale: A sign-off pushed into a queue competes with the contributor's actual job and loses, and by the time it surfaces their recall of the session has faded, so the review becomes a cold reading rather than a confirmation. Meanwhile the ticket sits blocked, and the team eventually starts treating silence as agreement, which is how a ticket reaches development carrying a misunderstanding nobody ever assented to.

rule.statement: BA opens the session with a pre-filled ticket template (title, type, parent epic, AC shell); blank-canvas drafting wastes session time.
rule.rationale: A blank ticket spends the scarcest resource in the room, the contributor's synchronous attention, on structural decisions the BA could have made alone the day before. The blank canvas also invites the session to drift into open discussion, because nothing visible is pulling the conversation toward the specific fields that still lack answers.

rule.statement: Each ticket draft MUST be timeboxed (default 8 minutes); over-running triggers a 'park or commit' decision, not silent over-run.
rule.rationale: Left unbounded, the single most contested ticket absorbs the session and the remaining ones are rushed at the end or never reached, which means the agenda was prioritised by accident. The timebox does not make the hard ticket easier; it forces the over-run to surface as an explicit choice to park it or commit to a rougher version, taken deliberately by the room rather than by the clock.

rule.statement: If ambiguity remains, the ticket MUST contain an explicit `[NEEDS-CLARIFICATION]` marker plus the owner of the clarification; silent ambiguity forbidden.
rule.rationale: An unresolved question written as ordinary prose is indistinguishable from a settled decision by the time a developer reads it, so it gets resolved during implementation, silently and usually in the cheapest direction. A fixed marker makes open questions countable and searchable across the whole backlog instead of findable only by reading everything. Naming the owner is the other half: an unassigned marker records that someone was uncomfortable, not that anyone will resolve it.

rule.statement: Session ends with a one-screen summary of all drafted tickets + their states (signed-off, needs-clarification, parked); summary persisted to engagement log.
rule.rationale: Participants leave a working session holding different beliefs about what was actually settled, and that divergence is cheapest to catch in the last two minutes while everyone is still present. The one-screen state makes the mismatch visible instead of leaving it to surface as a dispute at delivery. Persisting it to the engagement log is what lets that later disagreement be settled against a record rather than two confident memories.

rule.statement: Session is either recorded (with consent) or transcribed minutes are produced; pure verbal sign-off without artefact forbidden.
rule.rationale: A verbal sign-off that leaves no artefact reduces a later scope dispute to one party's memory against another's, and in a client relationship the vendor loses that exchange by default. The artefact does not have to be a recording, which is why minutes are an equal option: consent is not always available, and recording without it creates a confidentiality problem larger than the one it was meant to solve.

rule.statement: If contributors are async-only or screen-share is prohibited, return `skipped`.
rule.rationale: The entire value here is the synchronous correction loop. Where contributors are async-only there is no loop to close, and the pattern degrades into ordinary async drafting with an extra meeting attached. Where client security policy forbids screen sharing the mechanism simply is not available, and engineering a workaround trades a modest process gain for a policy violation on the client's own systems.
